## The personal AI computer

Zain Javaid is 19 years old, previously worked as a quantitative trader and has raised around 9.8 million euros in seed funding, an early financing round, for his start-up Ghost. Andreessen Horowitz leads the round, with Abstract, Audacious Ventures, SV Angel and Nova also participating. The product is called Core. Ghost describes it as a personal AI computer that runs local models entirely on the device around the clock. [...] The open models Qwen 3.8-Next, Qwen 3.8-27B, Gemma 4-31B and Muse-Glimmer-30B are preinstalled. According to Javaid, models with up to around 30 billion parameters, the model’s adjustable values, run entirely on the graphics card. Larger models such as Qwen-3.8-Next offload some parts to RAM.

TechCrunch reports that Ghost came out of stealth on 5 October 2026, with an $11 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Its product is Core, a $3,499 computer that Ghost’s website describes as a personal AI computer that “runs models entirely on device.” Ghost’s own pages add a second layer: its support page says Core still needs an internet connection for web search, email and software updates. This publication read Ghost’s website and privacy policy and TechCrunch’s report, tested nothing, and verified none of the claims independently.

   A new startup has built an AI PC which has sold out of its first batch
   Ghost's Core is a 'personal AI computer that runs models entirely on device'
   It connects to your apps, services and devices, so it 'builds context on your life over time, and works continuously to help you'

  

Ghost is a startup in the AI field that wants to capitalize on the desire to have agents running locally rather than using AI in the cloud — and to get this done with a minimum of fuss.

TechCrunch reports that Ghost's first product is a PC for using local AI agents which runs those LLMs (Large Language Models) exclusively on-device, ensuring your data stays private (I'll come back to that point later). [...] As well as the ease of use, privacy is the other big selling point for Core. It's tapping into a market of the increasing number of people realizing the potential of AI for helping with their life or work, who are concerned about sending their thoughts or data into the cloud, when they have no real idea where those queries or uploads will end up.

Core will run your AI agents continuously taking on whatever tasks you require while keeping all your data on the device, with Ghost promising that it's not going anywhere else. The personal data on the PC is encrypted to keep it safe — even Ghost can't access the data — and the device is specifically designed to keep running even if Ghost were to shut down (there's no subscription fee here).

# Ghost Core: The $3,499 Personal AI Computer That Runs Models On Device

Local AI, Hardware, Personal AI, Privacy, AI News

Ghost Core is a $3,499 personal AI computer running Qwen, Gemma and Muse models locally, 24/7, no subscription. What is known, what is not.

·9 min read·Yash Thakker

add explainx.ai
go deep

Ghost has launched Core, a personal AI computer priced at $3,499 that runs its models entirely on the device, with no subscription. Batch 1 is already sold out, and the product page now asks visitors to register interest for the next one. The pitch is a single line: "Intelligence you own." [...] | Question | Short answer |
 --- |
| What is it? | A dedicated personal AI computer that runs open-weight models locally and continuously |
| Price? | $3,499, no subscription |
| Can I buy one? | Batch 1 is sold out; you can register interest |
| Which models? | Qwen 3.8-Next, Qwen 3.8-27B, Gemma 4-31B, Muse-Glimmer-30B |
| Specs? | Not published on the launch page; GPU, CPU, memory and storage are listed without values |
| Does data leave the device? | Ghost says no; this is unverified |
| Returns? | 30-day returns |
| What does it connect to? | Email, calendar, finances, files, recordings, browser, lights, fridge, speaker, cameras, health records, Whoop, Oura, Eight Sleep |
| Is it proactive? | Yes, by design; it surfaces suggestions without being asked | [...] ## Is a proactive AI what you actually want?

The demo nudges are mild: bring an apple, drink water, check the weather. The harder question is where proactive help stops being useful and starts being intrusive. A message that notes you are most stressed on Sunday nights, or that you have eaten tacos for four days, treats your behavior as data to comment on. Some people will find that valuable. Others will find it unsettling, even if everything stays on a local drive.

The practical test is control. Can you set the topics Core may raise? Can you mute categories, delete what it has inferred, and see why it said something? A good proactive system explains itself and is easy to quiet. The launch material does not show those controls, so reserve judgment.
